steps.title: Pinot Noir
steps.body: Pinot Noir is about two-thirds of the Willamette Valley's vineyards. It gives bright red cherry, raspberry, cranberry and earthy, forest floor notes, with fresh acidity and silky tannins. It's often described as between Burgundy and California in style: riper than Burgundy, fresher than California.

steps.title: Whites and rules
steps.body: Pinot Gris, planted by David Lett in 1966, became Oregon's signature white: richer than Italian Pinot Grigio, with pear and spice. Chardonnay, once a struggle, is now excellent, using Dijon clones. Oregon requires 90% of a named grape on the label, stricter than the US federal 75%, for most varieties.
Oregon's 90% rule means a bottle labelled Pinot Noir is almost entirely Pinot Noir, unlike the 75% minimum elsewhere in the US.

steps.prompt: What share of a named grape does Oregon require on most labels?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinot Noir is about two-thirds of vineyards
Pinot Gris and Chardonnay are its key whites
Oregon requires 90% of a named grape
